We investigate the problem of solving the Schrödinger eigenvalue problem in a high-dimensional space using neural networks, where the potential energy is the sum of functions of each coordinate. Our study demonstrates that the ground state of the Schrödinger equation can be expressed as the product of functions of individual variables in the high-dimensional space. Our findings also show that the neural network model can be simplified to a small finite system of equations, enabling efficient computation of the first K eigenpairs in the high-dimensional space. Our numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of this approach.

The highest energy cosmic rays detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory exhibit significant anisotropy patterns, with the most prominent ones appearing at energies exceeding 4 EeV. These patterns are characterized by large-scale fluctuations in the cosmic-ray arrival directions, with the most pronounced effect being a pronounced dipole pattern. This dipole pattern, with an amplitude of approximately 5%, is consistent with previous findings and can be attributed to a combination of factors, including the distribution of cosmic-ray sources and the magnetic fields they encounter. In addition to the dipole pattern, the data also reveal a quadrupole pattern with an amplitude of approximately 2.5%, as well as other smaller-scale anisotropy patterns. These findings provide valuable insights into the origins and propagation of the highest energy cosmic rays, and may help to constrain models of their propagation through the universe.

We're examining a thin-layer homogenization problem within a specific 3D space framework. This problem involves a domain with multiple, very thin layers embedded in it, characterized by incommensurable periodic structures and isotropic properties. Our analysis reveals that as the layer thickness approaches zero, the solution to the problem converges to a unique, overarching solution in the main body of the framework, which is accompanied by a distinct layer solution. This solution is influenced by effective parameters derived from the periodic unit cell's properties.

We've developed an approach to define the self-interacting Dirac field within the FLRW spacetime using a real-time, non-perturbative method. By employing a self-consistent technique, we've established a way to calculate the effective mass of the Dirac particle through the self-energy. Our results show that the self-interaction causes the effective mass to oscillate in relation to the spacetime's scale factor. Additionally, we've found that the mode function of the Dirac particle is influenced by the self-interaction, causing deviations from the free theory mode function.

The categorization of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in whole-slide images is crucial for understanding cancer progression and selecting appropriate treatments. A novel approach has been developed to train a model that identifies categories of TILs in whole-slide images without the need for manual annotations. This method leverages the availability of whole-slide images and corresponding category information, circumventing the need for expert-annotated image patches. A tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte categorization task was chosen to test this method, given the scarcity of annotated whole-slide images in cancer research. A method that combines global feature extraction and attention mechanisms was proposed to address this challenge. This method was evaluated on a breast cancer dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying TIL categories in whole-slide images. The proposed method was also compared to existing approaches, highlighting its potential to improve cancer diagnosis and treatment by automating TIL categorization.

Cavity magnomechanics leverages the properties of two-dimensional magnetic substances to create complex systems involving magnons, phonons, and photons. This unique approach enables researchers to develop innovative quantum technologies. In this study, we propose a cavity magnomechanical system utilizing a single layer of magnetic substance and demonstrate its capability to generate two-dimensional entangled states of magnons and phonons. Our findings reveal that applying a mechanical drive to the substrate can enhance the system's entanglement. Furthermore, we investigate the dynamics of magnomechanical entanglement and identify conditions under which it persists. Our research also shows that the frequency of the mechanical drive can be used to control the direction of entanglement flow. In addition, we explore the generation of quantum correlations in the system and find that the magnomechanical entanglement is more robust than quantum correlations. Our findings provide a foundation for cavity magnomechanical quantum technology and may contribute to the development of new applications in this field.

In recent years, quadrupedal robots have garnered significant interest due to their potential applications in complex and challenging environments. A major obstacle in developing versatile quadrupedal robots is the creation of movement patterns that can adapt to various terrains. To overcome this limitation, a novel framework has been introduced that utilizes an evolutionary pathway creator to design training paths for reinforcement learning. By leveraging this pathway creation technique, the generated training environments enable the robots to learn more efficient motion patterns. Moreover, the framework employs a transfer learning approach to facilitate the adaptation of learned movement patterns to new robots. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this framework in designing training pathways and successfully transferring the learned movement patterns to different quadrupedal robots.

The low-luminosity active galactic core in NGC 7213 was observed using the X-ray Integral Field Unit on the XMM-Newton satellite, and the observations were analyzed using high-resolution spectral data.  The data revealed a broad Fe K$\alpha$ emission line with a full width at half maximum of 1000 km s$^{-1}$, which is significantly wider than the narrow Fe K$\alpha$ line observed in the on-axis spectrum.  This broad emission line is attributed to X-ray illumination of a warm, rotating accretion disk, and the width of the line suggests that the inner radius of the illuminated disk is approximately 1000 gravitational radii from the supermassive black hole.  This is consistent with the expectation that the X-ray emission from the accretion flow extends far beyond the standard innermost stable circular orbit.

A novel two-phase reinforcement learning method has been proposed to adjust a nonlinear controller without needing a pre-designed model. In the initial phase, the reinforcement learning algorithm optimizes a reward function that measures the nonlinear controller's performance, without requiring a pre-defined model. Subsequently, in the second phase, the reinforcement learning algorithm fine-tunes its policy using a linear model of the system, obtained through the nonlinear model's linearization around the optimal operating point. The suggested approach was tested on a real-world DC-DC converter and demonstrated the ability to switch between different operating points and adapt to changes in system parameters, all without needing a pre-defined model.

The SiD sensor, a key component of the upgraded Belle II detector, will utilize a unique approach to track particles by integrating the entire tracking system into the calorimeter's structure. To enhance tracking capabilities, particularly for particles that emit significant radiation, the SiD sensor concept has been modified by incorporating a new type of tracking detector in the center of the tracking volume. This innovative tracking detector will be based on the technology of the Belle II's vertex detector, but will be optimized for tracking particles that emit radiation. To achieve this, the tracking detector will utilize a stack of 12 layers made of double-sided silicon sensors with a thickness of 100 micrometers and a pitch of 25 micrometers. To mitigate the effects of radiation damage, the detector will be protected by a tungsten shield. To verify the feasibility of this concept, the tracking performance of the SiD detector was simulated using the particle data group (PDG) test beam data, and the results show that the SiD detector can achieve an impressive tracking resolution of 0.0014 degrees for particles that emit radiation.

We analyzed the spectra of Tonantzintla 2, a bulge globular cluster, using high-resolution data from APOGEE. This cluster is located in the inner region of the Milky Way and has been identified as a double-star system with distinct stellar populations. Our study involved 12 stars from the redder population of Tonantzintla 2, which were observed using APOGEE during a separate survey. By comparing the spectra of these stars with those from a separate study, we found that the stars exhibit similar chemical compositions and metallicity levels. This suggests that the two populations in Tonantzintla 2 share a common origin and have undergone similar chemical evolution processes. Our study also revealed that the two populations in Tonantzintla 2 have distinct age and metallicity levels, which suggests that the two populations formed at different times and under different conditions. This research contributes to our understanding of the formation and evolution of globular clusters in the Milky Way and other galaxies.

The Earth is experiencing rapid changes, making it crucial to monitor the planet's health and well-being. To facilitate this, a network called EarthNets has been developed, which integrates data from various sources such as satellite imagery, ground-based sensors, and numerical models. By combining this data, EarthNets enables the analysis of the Earth's dynamics and the detection of patterns that can inform decision-making. To process the vast amounts of data generated by EarthNets, advanced AI techniques are employed, including machine learning and deep learning, which can analyze the data and make predictions about the Earth's future. To support the application of AI in planet monitoring, a set of reference datasets has been created, which includes data from various EarthNets sources and is available for research and development purposes.

Active nematics, a type of active matter, exhibit spontaneous flow characteristics even in the absence of external forces. Examples of active nematics include biological systems like the cytoskeleton and multicellular tissues. We employ a renormalization group approach to analyze the hydrodynamic behavior of 2D active nematics, focusing on how key parameters change over different scales. Our analysis reveals that certain fluctuations become more significant at larger scales, affecting the nematics' hydrodynamic behavior.

Identifying unusual patterns in data streams is a crucial task in real-time data analysis. However, existing methods often struggle with pinpointing anomalies within time-series information. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel approach called ReAD that leverages existing segmentation techniques to accurately localize anomalies in time-series data. By dividing the entire dataset into equal-length sections and assigning each a score, we can determine the overall normality of each section. These scores enable us to pinpoint sections containing anomalies and subsequently isolate subsections with high abnormality rates. Through rigorous experimentation on three distinct datasets, we demonstrate that our proposed technique surpasses existing alternatives in anomaly localization performance.

We've carried out a comprehensive study of the pion's vector form factor, focusing on its behavior across the entire energy spectrum, by incorporating both theoretical models and experimental data. This research also examines the potential impact of the pion's form factor on the precision calculation of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, with a particular emphasis on two-loop electroweak photon bubble diagrams involving charged pions.

Advancements in Large Language Models have enabled the creation of a versatile code-based LLM, referred to as a Universal Embodiment, which can execute multiple tasks across various physical and virtual environments through written instructions provided in the form of pseudocode. Our study introduces a new framework that empowers the model to interact with diverse physical settings, software interfaces, and programming languages, and even enables it to adapt to new ones with minimal exposure. Furthermore, we introduce the REACT-2 model, which exhibits robust performance in executing tasks within simulated 3D environments described by realistic Python-based physics simulations.

Our study investigates the relationship between galaxy shape and mass using a comprehensive dataset of 10,000 early-type galaxies from the SDSS. By analyzing the distribution of elliptical and lensed galaxies, we found that more massive galaxies have a higher proportion of elliptical shapes. This relationship holds true across different galaxy masses, with a notable shift in shape distribution observed for galaxies with masses greater than 10^11 solar masses. This shift is also evident in the distribution of dark matter halos, with more massive halos having a higher proportion of elliptical shapes. This supports the hypothesis that galaxy shape is influenced by the dynamics of dark matter halos, with a more massive halo having a higher proportion of elliptical shapes.

A new technique for monitoring aerosol optical depth (AOD) has been developed using existing photometric data and the brightness of stars. This innovative approach utilizes AOD measurements from the MODIS satellite to create real-time light curves for stars observed by amateur astronomers. By comparing observed to expected brightness, the MASTRODIA system can detect changes in stellar visibility caused by varying AOD. This method has the potential to provide continuous AOD monitoring, supplementing satellite data and providing insights into local atmospheric conditions.

The Graphical Lasso algorithm is a popular method for estimating the precision matrix in high-dimensional data sets, and the Python library GGLasso facilitates this process for various probability density functions, including multivariate Gaussian, Student-t, and multivariate Laplace distributions.

The development of planetary systems is influenced by the processes of planet formation and disk evolution, which can be observed through the development of planetary masses and the clearing of protoplanetary disks. To understand the underlying mechanisms, high-angular-resolution radio observations are required. This study presents a theoretical framework for radio continuum observations of a protoplanetary disk, incorporating the effects of photoevaporation and magnetohydrodynamic disk evolution. By comparing the predicted radio continuum spectra of a protoplanetary disk with observations of the star TW Hydrae, we can determine the most likely disk evolution model. Our analysis suggests that a photoevaporation model with a mass loss rate of 10^-14 M_sun/yr provides the best fit to the observed data, and that a magnetic disk evolution model is unlikely to explain the observations. This study highlights the importance of radio continuum observations in understanding disk evolution and the role of planet formation.

A speech processing system has been developed that automatically detects and classifies speech sounds without human intervention. This novel approach utilizes the principle of Occam's Razor to categorize speech sounds by evaluating the simplicity of two potential models - one for speech and one for silence - and determining which model best fits the input data. A new model is created for each possibility and their performance is assessed using dynamic data, with the model that best fits the data being selected. This classification system is complemented by a model that estimates the fundamental frequency of speech sounds, utilizing a previously established method. The effectiveness of this new categorization system and frequency estimation method has been demonstrated through experimentation on a speech database, showing that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and simplicity.

We introduce a new algorithm, dynamically weighted inertial forward-reverse, to solve monotone inclusion problems. By integrating the forward-reverse algorithm with a time-varying combination of the rock algorithm and the extra-antipodal algorithm, our method achieves global convergence under specific conditions. The addition of inertia and adaptive weighting further enhances its performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm through numerical experiments, showing it outperforms the proximal point algorithm and a forward-reverse algorithm with adaptive step sizes.

The New Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model is examined with two distinct mechanisms for generating neutrino masses: the standard and reverse seesaw models. Focusing on loop corrections to the Higgs mass, we analyze the models' predictions for neutrino masses and mixings, as well as their implications for the Higgs sector.

Achieving high performance in neural network design is a complex task, as the optimal architecture is influenced by numerous factors, including the training data, network structure, optimization techniques, and more. This variability makes it challenging to identify a universal design that consistently yields superior results. To address this issue, researchers have developed a two-part approach: first, they identify key design characteristics that impact the performance of neural networks, and then they utilize a synthesis method to systematically explore the design space, ensuring that all possible configurations are evaluated. This comprehensive search method guarantees the discovery of the best design, and our study demonstrates its effectiveness by outperforming top designs found through leading automated design search tools on various benchmark datasets.

In millimeter wave networks, the high potential for multi-group broadcasting is hindered by the need for frequent beam realignment. This realignment process is resource-intensive and can be costly. To address this issue, we propose a hybrid encoding scheme that combines network coding with beamforming to reduce the number of required beam realignments. This hybrid approach is evaluated in a 5G testbed environment, where it is compared to traditional beamforming and beamwidth reduction methods. The results show that the hybrid encoding scheme can significantly reduce the number of beam realignments and improve overall system performance.

In distributed machine learning, Federated Learning (FL) is an effective approach that enables communication between multiple parties without sharing sensitive data. However, the current implementation of FL is inefficient due to high communication costs and data privacy concerns, as it transmits raw model updates and uses insecure channels. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new federated model called Federated Factorization Machines (FFM), which enhances communication efficiency and safeguards party data by factorizing model updates and securely exchanging information through Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). Experimental results show that FFM outperforms traditional FFM and its encrypted variant in terms of accuracy and has the potential to be applied to other machine learning models.

In Next Generation Networks (NGN), Next-Generation Named Data Networking (NGNNDN) is an innovative approach to building a content-centric network that seamlessly integrates computing capabilities. The NDN architecture enables applications to utilize network resources as if they were local, but existing dynamic resource management tools are not compatible with NDN's data-driven framework. This paper presents a novel dynamic resource management strategy for NDN computing networks, which leverages Named Data Processing (NDP) to enable network elements to process and analyze network data. The proposed NDP-based strategy involves NDN routers collecting and analyzing network data, then processing it to generate insights that inform resource allocation and routing decisions. The goal is to maximize the network's overall content delivery rate while minimizing the data transmission cost. The proposed NDP-based strategy is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and solved using a model-based method. The results show that this strategy outperforms traditional NDN routing methods and an alternative MDP-based solution in terms of increased content delivery and reduced data transmission costs.

We examine the stability of an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam connected to p masses on a finite, undirected, planar, connected graph with a central hub and p branches of varying lengths. The beam and elastic masses interact on a star-shaped network, where we develop an approach to derive the resolvent operator for the associated infinite system. This approach enables us to establish sufficient conditions for the system's complete stability and proves that the conditions are both necessary and sufficient in certain cases.

Incorporating the $U(1)_A$-symmetry breaking into the quark-meson model allows for a more accurate representation of the physical quark content. This study investigates the impact of explicit $U(1)_A$-symmetry breaking on the chiral phase transition by introducing the explicit breaking term with an appropriate coefficient. The results show that increasing the explicit $U(1)_A$-symmetry breaking coefficient leads to a more complex phase diagram with multiple phases. A critical threshold for the $U(1)_A$-symmetry breaking coefficient is identified, beyond which the chiral phase transition shifts from being of the second order to the first order. Furthermore, a novel mixed phase emerges when the explicit $U(1)_A$-symmetry breaking coefficient exceeds this critical threshold, characterized by a combination of chirally restored quark matter and $U(1)_A$-symmetry restored quark-meson state.

The discovery of topological insulators with large band gaps has been a long-standing goal in condensed matter physics research. Recent findings have revealed a new class of large band gap topological insulators, the novel compound MTl4Te3 (M = Cd, Hg). Theoretical analysis has shown that these materials exhibit a band gap of 0.20 eV and 0.24 eV, respectively. The study of the electronic properties of these topological insulators has been conducted using first-principles calculations. The results indicate that the materials exhibit strong spin-orbit coupling and the spin texture of the surface states conforms to Dirac dispersion. The stability of the materials has been confirmed through the analysis of the phonon dispersion and the electron-phonon coupling. The study of the optical properties of the materials has also been conducted.

In real-world applications, utility functions are frequently employed to translate abstract objectives into measurable parameters. However, their use is often hindered by difficulties in accurately assessing all parameters and dealing with conflicting goals. We propose a novel approach that learns a utility function directly from example data, enabling optimization without the need for further human input. Our method is demonstrated on two complex problems: designing an aircraft wing and optimizing its engine, where we show that it can successfully identify an effective utility function and find the best solutions, even with limited human input.

Recent breakthroughs in reinforcement learning have enabled the development of sophisticated agents capable of tackling intricate tasks. However, these agents can be susceptible to deceptive countermeasures, such as those leveraging internal knowledge of the agent's structure. To counter this limitation, this study investigates a new class of blackbox attacks that exploit temporal information processing within the agent's reinforcement learning framework. These attacks utilize custom-designed time-series data to manipulate the agent's behavior, with two proposed attack methods - one targeting Q-learning agents and another targeting proximal policy optimization agents - demonstrating significant effectiveness in inducing malicious actions in their respective target scenarios.

Within the 17 non-symmetric architectural classes, the behavior of electrons within certain three-dimensional crystals has been thoroughly examined, but the electron behavior in 2D crystals has received less attention. In this study, we examine the electron behavior in 2D crystals that belong to two specific structural categories, showcasing a unique type of quantum lattice that exhibits Dirac points in its electron spectrum. These Dirac points can be manipulated by adjusting a specific property of the lattice, resulting in a unique type of quantum state. Additionally, we demonstrate that by introducing a specific type of electron interaction, the electron behavior within this lattice can be controlled, leading to the emergence of specific types of quantum states that can be utilized in the development of advanced electronic devices.

This research focuses on developing an advanced risk-conscious reinforcement learning method for minimizing the chance of rare but significant failures in complex systems with changing failure probabilities. A novel risk metric based on failure probability is proposed, and its properties are examined in relation to the failure frequency. A dynamic failure tracking method, known as the resentment mechanism, is introduced to effectively capture this frequency in real-time. A novel risk value function is designed by integrating the resentment mechanism with the traditional risk assessment, and its optimality is demonstrated. A risk-aware reinforcement learning algorithm is then developed based on this function and proven to converge to the optimal solution with high probability. Furthermore, the algorithm's ability to separate state estimation, policy optimization, and failure frequency tracking is demonstrated, and the resulting identification design is shown to be optimal.

The development of software projects heavily relies on issue tracking systems, which facilitate the organization and monitoring of tasks and issues.  A widely used issue tracking platform, Jira, allows project managers to monitor tasks and issues, enabling them to identify and address problems that may arise during the development process.  To effectively manage these tasks and issues, project managers utilize various tracking methods, such as labeling, categorizing, and assigning issues to team members.  To gain insights into the problem tracking practices of software development teams, researchers have analyzed public Jira repositories to understand how these teams label, categorize, and assign issues.  To further this research, we present an alternate collection of public Jira repositories, which we used to study the problem tracking practices of software development teams.

In distributed machine learning, the efficiency and accuracy of training models are heavily influenced by network latency and data heterogeneity. A key challenge lies in finding an optimal aggregation function that can minimize the impact of these factors. We've identified a specific class of functions, known as piece-wise linear functions with two segments, that can effectively balance model convergence and communication costs. By optimizing the slope of these functions, we can improve the performance of machine learning models in various scenarios, including data-driven and network-driven situations. Our research demonstrates that this new aggregation function class can achieve optimal results with minimal communication and under diverse data distributions.

A proposed integrated system captures and manipulates a single atom using multiple beams of different diffraction patterns. The diffraction beams trap the atom at stable points, where optical traps are used to control the atom's position. The setup also allows for measuring the atom's state by analyzing its fluorescence, which is collected and measured using a detector. The uniformity of the diffraction patterns facilitates efficient data collection, and the entire system is designed to be compact and scalable for experiments with multiple atoms.

The $\bold\Lambda^{\ast}$ structure, a monoid generated by a set of letters $\bold\Lambda$, is a fundamental concept in theoretical computer science and formal language theory. In this study, we present a new method to determine the MacNeille fulfillment of this monoid structure, building on previous work that established a MacNeille fulfillment for the $\bold\Lambda^{\ast}$ order. Our method involves constructing a tree-based order and demonstrating its equivalence to the $\bold\Lambda^{\ast}$ order through a series of proofs.

This paper outlines a novel approach for deducing the polymer structure from the
theoretical model's parameters, specifically the Flory-Freeman-Fox equation, that
correlates molecular weight with viscosity. Our proposed method leverages the
whole programming technique to find the integer values of the polymer structure
that minimize the discrepancy between the equation's theoretical predictions and
the experimentally determined molecular weights and viscosities. We demonstrate
the feasibility of this method by applying it to a dataset comprising 1000
unique polymer entries.

This article presents a collection of techniques for real-time audio signal enhancement, enabling the creation of high-quality audio from low-fi sources. We offer practical examples and a step-by-step guide, along with an open-source implementation, to facilitate the adoption of these technologies. In addition, we showcase a case study featuring our work on enhanced breathing sounds from COVID-19 patients, which can be utilized for educational purposes.

For a rational function f, we define the set of points whose forward orbits eventually become periodic under f as Fat(f). We then consider the case where f is a rational function on the projective plane, with two critical points, and investigate the group generated by the actions of f on the projective plane, the projective line, and the set of points not in Fat(f) of the projective plane.

In high-dimensional linear regression, our goal is to estimate unknown parameters and the associated uncertainty in the error variance. We focus on two specific types of prior distributions - one that accounts for the skewness of the error distribution and another that reflects our uncertainty about the prior's concentration. By combining these distributions, we can derive the marginal distribution of the error, which allows us to model skewed errors and unknown concentration simultaneously. We develop a Bayesian estimator for the error variance and establish its accuracy under certain conditions. We also examine the performance of this estimator in the presence of model uncertainty and establish its accuracy under certain conditions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and real-world data analysis.

In the manufacturing sector, machining centers are a fundamental component, 
yet their energy efficiency is not thoroughly investigated. To address this gap, 
a research approach is presented that involves modeling machining centers as 
virtual entities and identifying the most energy-efficient hubs through an 
optimized assessment. To achieve this, Bayesian evaluation is employed to 
calculate the probability of each machining hub's optimal energy efficiency, 
followed by refining this probability using a genetic algorithm to enhance 
accuracy. Ultimately, a probability metric is developed to rank the machining 
centers based on their energy efficiency, allowing for the identification of 
hubs with the highest potential for efficiency.

This theory is further explored in a paper that examines the conditions under which a unique conformal measure exists on a graph, based on a condition that relates the conformal dimension to the spectral dimension. This condition is part of a broader theory that relates the spectral dimension to the fractal dimension of a set. This study investigates the impact of η-η' blending on phase behavior and miscibility gaps in binary and ternary polymer mixtures. Focusing on styrene (η) and methyl methacrylate (η') monomers, researchers utilized the Flory-Huggins theory to analyze the phase diagrams of polymer blends. By incorporating experimental interaction parameters, the study successfully predicted the miscibility gaps in various polymer mixtures, including those of poly(η-co-η') with polystyrene and poly(methyl methacrylate). The research also explored the critical composition and temperature of these polymer blends, revealing that η-η' blending can induce reentrant miscibility gaps and alter the nature of the phase transition.

This research aims to assess the reliability of signature-based online authentication systems by examining the distinctiveness, complexity, and coherence of signatures from 100 individuals signing 25 times each online. The study's findings indicate that human signatures are characterized by variability in both inter-signature and intra-signature contexts. Furthermore, the study reveals that the complexity of signing motions is influenced by the size of the signing area, and the act of signing is not entirely independent of mouse movements.

We investigated the four-loop perturbations in the super Yang-Mandel theory, specifically the skew-N=6 symmetric sectors, and found that certain elevated-derivative terms do not exhibit divergence. This research builds upon a previous study on skew-N=6 symmetric sectors, where we discovered the absence of four-loop anomalies. This finding led us to examine the terms with the highest degree of derivatives in the skew-N=6 sector's action. Our analysis revealed the absence of four-loop anomalies for two specific types of elevated-derivative terms, indicating their potential inclusion in the action as finite corrections.

Theoretical models of spin deflection by a stationary charge suggest that spin deflection is primarily due to the magnetic interaction, with secondary effects from electric charge, relativistic effects, and time-based interactions being negligible. However, in higher-order interactions, the magnetic and electric effects can switch places, with the latter dominating in certain scenarios. This study investigates the spin deflection of electrons and holes by a positively charged defector, using a simplified model that incorporates relativistic effects, and finds that the spin deflection is influenced by the type of defector and the particle's velocity, with the magnetic and electric effects switching places when the particle's velocity exceeds a certain threshold.

The creation of elements in the universe is a fundamental process that is
investigated through the lens of nuclear physics. The study of this process
is constrained by the scarcity of specific isotopes, which are essential for
understanding how elements are formed. The research presented here focuses on
the creation of nitrogen isotopes, which are crucial for comprehending the
universe's elemental composition. The study involves the measurement of nuclear
reactions that are thought to be responsible for the creation of these isotopes,
which are carried out using a sophisticated experimental setup. The results of
these experiments provide new insights into the nuclear physics of these
isotopes and place limits on the creation of nitrogen in the universe.

This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the difficulties and considerations associated with code-mixing and code-switching in Natural Language Processing (NLP). We examine the motivations behind obstacles like bilingual education, social pressures, and cultural identity, which give rise to code-mixing and code-switching. We also explore the challenges and opportunities associated with these phenomena in the context of NLG and other NLP tasks.

In biomedical research, visual representations of complex networks are essential for understanding intricate relationships. Graph depiction learning focuses on translating these visual images into a numerical format that can be used for analysis and further study. This task is particularly important in biomedical applications where graph images convey critical information about biological processes and interactions. By converting graph depiction images into a numerical representation, researchers can leverage the power of deep learning techniques to uncover hidden patterns and insights. This chapter delves into the latest advancements in graph depiction learning, highlighting its applications in biomedical fields and providing a comprehensive overview of the underlying methodologies and techniques.

We've investigated the potential for inelastic dark matter and left-right symmetrical models to be detected through enhanced xenon in direct detection experiments. Our research shows that inelastic scattering can still be detected with a lower threshold than previously thought, potentially allowing for the inelastic $\chi$ component of a mixed $\chi$-$Z'$ dark matter model to be discovered by next-generation xenon detectors. Furthermore, we've found that the xenon detection range for the inelastic $\chi$ component of this model exceeds that of the spin-dependent proton channel with nuclear recoil thresholds of 10 keV. Our study also reveals that the xenon detection range for the $W_R$ in a left-right symmetrical model with $M_{SUSY} = 1$ TeV and $v_R = 10^{10}$ GeV surpasses that of WIMP neutralino annihilation through the Z boson in xenon detectors with 1 tonne-year exposure.

This research introduces a graph privacy consultant, a system designed to safeguard sensitive information within graph datasets. By analyzing various suppression techniques, the consultant identifies the most effective method to eliminate specified subsets of data while adhering to a predefined privacy threshold. Our consultant utilizes a combination of edge suppression and noise addition to eliminate data points, ensuring that it can accurately remove any subset of edges within a graph dataset. To validate its performance, the consultant was tested on both synthetic and real-world graph datasets, demonstrating its ability to consistently meet the required privacy standards.

This paper explores the properties of purity in the context of toric Calabi-Yau 3-folds from a mathematical perspective. We develop a novel framework for identifying and categorizing these folds based on the presence of a 'hidden purity' structure. Our research involves creating a new method to represent these folds using 'concealed' diagrams, which we then apply to a specific class of 1-parameter families of 3-folds known as toric del Pezzo surfaces. We also introduce an innovative approach to calculating the 'conformal dimension' of these families and establish a new relationship between a 'hidden purity' structure and this dimension. Our findings confirm a previously established mathematical connection between these folds and a specific type of geometric object, providing further evidence for this relationship.

Fragmentation properties of light quarks and gluons in proton-proton and nucleus-nucleus interactions are investigated using the ATLAS experiment at the LHC. Fragmentation patterns are studied in single-proton and lead-lead events from 2012 and 2013 data sets, corresponding to a total of 25.3 fb^-1 for proton-proton and 273 nb^-1 for lead-lead collisions. Fragmentation of high transverse momentum particles is examined in proton-proton events at 7 and 13 TeV, and in lead-lead events at 2.76 TeV with a nuclear modification factor of less than 0.1. High-performance computing has greatly benefited from advances in quantum chemistry simulations, particularly with the development of the ab initio simulation package CP2K. By integrating quantum mechanics and molecular mechanics, CP2K enables efficient modeling of large systems, including those with long-range electrostatic interactions. The code's success is attributed to its utilization of the Fast Fourier Transform and its adaptability to various hardware architectures. This article highlights recent CP2K developments, including the implementation of the planar wave method on Intel Xeon Phi processors and the inclusion of the isodensity grid for property analysis in PyMOL.

Coronal hard X-ray emission is primarily caused by the rapid deceleration of high-energy electrons in the sun's upper atmosphere, and this phenomenon is a key indicator of the energy release in solar flares.  The rate of this emission is proportional to the square of the number of interacting particles, meaning that weaker signals can be produced by a smaller number of high-energy electrons interacting with a larger population of stationary particles.  The detection of such faint signals is essential for understanding the overall energy release in solar flares.  The FOXSI instrument, which is part of the NuSTAR satellite, has been able to observe the sun's upper atmosphere in the energy range of 6-30 keV, and has detected coronal hard X-ray emission from the sun during the event of May 14, 2022.  The observations revealed a coronal emission of approximately 10^-4 times the brightness of the sun's typical flare emissions, and this signal was detected in the FOXSI 3-6 and 6-12 keV bands.  The coronal emission was found to be located in the active region of the sun, and its intensity was found to be consistent with the predictions of solar flare models.  The detection of such faint signals is a significant achievement for the FOXSI instrument, and it has important implications for our understanding of the energy release in solar flares.

Predicting the social influence of technology innovations is crucial for making informed policy decisions. In this research, we investigate how to forecast the social impact of innovations using time-expanded graphs and graph neural networks. We develop an approach to predict the social impact of technology innovations over time, taking into consideration the temporal dynamics and policy restrictions. We train and evaluate graph neural models on these time-expanded graphs to predict the social impact of technology innovations over different time periods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a dataset of train and ride-hailing services in San Francisco, showing that our model can accurately predict the social impact of these innovations over different time periods and under various policy scenarios.

Our research explores the intricacy of geometric field theories using Euler-Arnold equations and spectral analysis. We start by defining geometric field theories within the context of infinite-dimensional homogeneous spaces and their corresponding dual pairs of momentum maps. Next, we reduce the Euler-Arnold hydrodynamic type equations for these theories to finite-dimensional models and compute their Lyapunov spectra. We then illustrate our approach with examples, including the field theory described in da Costa's 2021 study and a new example involving maps from 2D spatial domains to 3D spheres.

In object pose estimation, we aim to identify the optimal position and orientation of a 3D model that best fits observed images. This process is crucial for various applications, including medical imaging, where accurate model placement is essential. Recent advances in image synthesis have enabled the creation of high-quality 3D models from two images, but their use in pose estimation is hindered by inaccuracies. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages all available data points to accurately determine object pose. By utilizing the distribution of residuals, our method can identify and exclude outliers, thereby improving the robustness of pose estimation. Our approach outperforms existing methods in both speed and accuracy, as demonstrated by our experimental results on simulated and real-world datasets.

The early universe's rapid expansion may have led to a situation where different physical conditions coexisted due to separate inflationary periods. We're focusing on a scenario where a significant portion of the universe's energy density was hidden from the standard model particles, potentially affecting the universe's cooling rate and the cosmic microwave background radiation we observe today. This hidden sector could consist of particles interacting with standard model particles through a mediator, leading to a situation where the universe can be seen as having multiple temperatures. We're using a simplified model to study this scenario and determine the limits on hidden sector properties based on our current understanding of the universe's composition and the cosmic microwave background radiation.

Researchers have conducted an examination of the rare occurrence of same-sign W boson pairs at the CERN LHC, using a substantial dataset of 36 fb$^{-1}$ collected at a proton-proton collision energy of 13 TeV. The analysis involved searching for signs of electroweak production of W boson pairs, focusing on events with two same-sign W bosons, jets, and two identical charged leptons along with missing transverse momentum. The findings were compared against predictions from the Standard Model, revealing no significant signs of new physics. The data were then used to establish the most restrictive limits on electroweak W boson pair production, specifically within a range of two jet and two identical lepton events at a 95% confidence level.

Our research focuses on developing an efficient method for colorizing black and white images from surveillance cameras, especially those that have suffered color degradation due to long-term use. To achieve this, we propose an innovative approach called Cross-Camera Profound Colorization (CCPC), which leverages the color information from an existing color camera to enhance the quality of colorization in a degraded black and white camera. The proposed method consists of two main components: a B&W to color mapping network that translates black and white pixel values to corresponding color triplets, and a B&W color consistency verification network that ensures the generated color images match the black and white input. The novelty of our approach lies in its ability to utilize data from a color camera, thereby eliminating the need for B&W to color pairs during training. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in generating accurate and realistic color images.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of a specific type of mathematical model, known as the $\Lambda$CDM model, to see if it accurately describes the structure of space. By examining various datasets, including measurements of cosmic distances and patterns of light from distant galaxies, we found that the $\Lambda$CDM model is likely correct. However, when combining these datasets, we found that the model doesn't perfectly match other evidence, such as the pattern of fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background, suggesting that there may be additional factors at play. We also explored alternative models and found that they don't provide a better fit to the data.

On GitHub, the primary method for modifying files is through pull requests, which are typically created when the contents of a file have genuinely changed. However, some PRs involve updating metadata, such as adding comments or changing version numbers, without altering the actual content. Although these PRs may seem insignificant, they can be useful for tracking changes like software updates or maintenance activities. Currently, the analysis of these PRs is limited, as most studies only examine the content of files. To address this limitation, we have developed a new approach that utilizes NLP to identify PRs that modify metadata, allowing us to better understand their impact and benefits.

BD+20 2357 is an exceptional eclipsing binary system consisting of two nearly equal-sized stars, classified as BD Doradus variables. By utilizing the long-term TESS data, we analyzed the system's behavior and discovered significant variability in its amplitude and frequency. This variability is attributed to the interaction between the stars and the presence of starspots. By applying the Wilson-Devinney code, we determined the stars' physical properties and found that they are slightly larger than the Sun, with surface temperatures of around 5500 Kelvin. Our analysis also revealed that the system's pulsation periods are consistent with the BD Doradus range, and that the more massive star is the likely pulsator. Our findings provide valuable insights into the evolution of binary systems and the role of binary interactions in BD Doradus stars.

The Yamabe equation in fractional conformal geometry has a specific equation that can be solved using an associated flow known as the fractional Yamabe flow. This equation and flow are based on Riemannian manifolds and are defined using nonlocal operators. Our research focuses on the existence of a globally smooth, positive solution to this equation, which is guaranteed for a specific class of initial conditions.

The surge in online shopping has led to an overwhelming number of product choices, making it difficult for users to select the ideal product. Recommendation systems can help by offering tailored suggestions, but they often fall short in providing in-depth product insights. To address this, we introduce an innovative approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain recommendation, which considers product and user preferences across multiple product characteristics. This approach aims to provide users with more comprehensive product information and a better understanding of their tastes. To achieve this, we propose a novel Thorough Aspect Preference Learning (TAPL) model that incorporates an aspect-based recommendation framework. This framework is designed to learn user and product characteristics across multiple dimensions, enabling aspect-aware recommendation. To further enhance the model's performance, we introduce an Aspect Regularization (AR) module that improves the generalization of aspect preferences. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our model over existing baseline methods.

We investigate the first-order deformation spaces of mixed symplectic and
symplectic orthogonal bundles over a smooth algebraic surface, establishing a
precise description of this space and demonstrating its relationship to the
configuration spaces of isotropic 2-planes in symplectic vector spaces.

Let D_k(n) be the count of ways to divide the set {1, 2,..., n} into sets with a count of elements that are multiples of k and have a size of less than k. We provide a formula for D_k(n) and a recursive relationship for it.

This study examines the stability of least squares estimation when using noisy data samples. We consider a scenario where an unknown parameter is estimated by utilizing $n$ data points, each influenced by noise with variance $\sigma^2$. We demonstrate that with $n$ data points exceeding $100\sigma^2$, an estimator based on sample data can accurately approximate the true value within $1+\epsilon$ relative error with high probability. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound indicating that $n$ data points should be at least $2\sigma^2$ to achieve such an estimator. We also investigate the minimum number of data points required for an estimator to achieve this approximation, considering different noise models including sub-Gaussian, bounded, and adversarial conditions.

Recent advancements in precision measurements of the X(3872) have enabled researchers to examine its movement in the mass spectrum. This analysis focuses on the LHC's potential to provide insights into the X(3872)'s nature through the study of its production in high-energy proton-proton collisions. Theoretical predictions for the X(3872)'s production rate in such processes are based on non-relativistic QCD, a framework that describes the behavior of quarks and gluons. The predictions are found to be consistent with current experimental data, suggesting a need for further investigation. The study also considers the potential of the X(3872)'s spin-dependent production in decays of the $B_c$ and the charmonium system to provide constraints on its properties. The predictions for the X(3872) and $B_c$ are found to be within the reach of the LHC, suggesting that the LHC has the potential to provide insights into the X(3872)'s nature through the study of its production and decays.

The occurrence of local moments in disordered systems, specifically in the Hubbard model, has been investigated. Our research reveals that disorder in the system gives rise to rare regions, which behave as local Kondo hubs. These regions dominate system properties at low temperatures. Our findings indicate that local moments form as a result of disorder, contrary to what happens in clean systems where they are suppressed. The local density of states around these rare regions exhibits a zero-bias peak, which is a key feature of Kondo physics. This phenomenon is observed in both the disordered Hubbard model and a related random single-orbital model. Our study demonstrates that the local moment formation in disordered systems is a direct consequence of disorder itself.
This study extends the concepts of descent, descent set, and descent algebra from the symmetric group to the braid group, building upon the original work of Garsia and Sahi.

This research explores the properties of scalar field theories within a specific framework, similar to the well-known $\lambda\phi^4$ theory but differing in that it lacks a particular symmetry. We establish that within this theoretical framework, there exist distinct types of scalar field interactions, one of which is confirmed to be free of unwanted singularities. We then investigate the presence of stable, particle-like structures within these interactions, discovering that they exist in certain, but not all, of the scalar field interactions.

Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is a technique to infer a reward function from observed optimal behaviors in an environment. However, obtaining precise optimal trajectories can be challenging due to the need for high-precision sensors and the complexity of the underlying dynamics. A more practical approach is to identify a policy that explains the observed sub-optimal trajectories. Despite this, real-world data often contains noise, making it difficult to extract useful information. A new method is proposed to address these issues by using a hierarchical Bayesian approach that can simultaneously learn multiple reward functions, an observation model, and an underlying optimal policy from noisy, partial observations. The method leverages a hierarchical structure where multiple agents' perspectives are considered, with top-level rewards representing the optimal policy and lower-level observations being made by the system. The method employs Maximum Entropy iMLE to learn the reward functions and uses Gibbs sampling to estimate the posterior distribution over the system parameters. The method is demonstrated on a simulated grid-world and a real-world dataset of human navigation in an office environment.

The widespread use of autonomous vehicles in the future will heavily rely on advanced control systems, but their successful implementation is hindered by complex control problems, particularly in scenarios involving safety and smooth operation. To address this, we've developed a novel approach that integrates two deep reinforcement learning algorithms to tackle these challenges, with one algorithm ensuring safety and smoothness, and the other optimizing performance, such as energy efficiency. By leveraging the capabilities of deep reinforcement learning, we can effectively handle scenarios that are infeasible through traditional model-based methods, and our approach has been demonstrated to address the previously mentioned control issues, while also outperforming existing solutions in terms of energy efficiency.

We now investigate the growth of dark holes that are extremely massive, and how they relate to the massive objects that form in the universe. We use a mathematical model to simulate the evolution of dark holes, and find that dark holes in the universe can grow to be extremely massive, and their growth is influenced by the environment. The recent surge in deep learning has led to its widespread adoption in various scientific fields, including physics, where it has shown promise in analyzing complex data sets. However, despite its potential, deep learning's application in science is still in its infancy, and many scientists remain hesitant to use it due to its lack of transparency and reliability. To address these concerns, we have developed a novel approach that leverages deep learning to analyze real-world scientific data, specifically inelastic neutron scattering spectra. By incorporating interpretability and adaptability into our method, we can gain valuable insights into how deep learning models process and understand scientific data.

The rise of preprints has significantly altered the landscape of scientific research dissemination. Preprints are freely accessible documents that scientists can share with the public before undergoing peer review. This study examines the evolution of preprint servers from the 1980s to the present day, focusing on their development, operational procedures, and the communities surrounding them. By analyzing preprint data spanning three decades, we reveal the growth and diversity of preprint adoption across various scientific disciplines. Our analysis also highlights the correlation between preprint usage and the publication of research in high-impact journals. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of preprints as a means of facilitating open and accessible scientific communication.

Digital laboratory notebooks have been gaining traction in recent years, 
offering a range of digital formats to document experiments. 
Despite the numerous benefits of digital documentation, many researchers 
still rely on traditional paper-based laboratory notebooks. 
This study introduces a digital laboratory notebook solution designed to 
streamline data management and documentation within the lab environment. 
By integrating with existing lab processes, this notebook can be utilized 
both digitally and on paper, offering an option for printing entries when 
necessary. 
To assess the feasibility of this tool, we conducted a survey of researchers 
and found that while digital documentation is generally preferred, 
certain limitations hinder its widespread adoption. 
Our research notebook addresses these challenges by providing an adaptable 
documentation system that accommodates various lab workflows.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are emerging as a groundbreaking class of materials, characterized by their complex multi-principal element composition. The intricate atomic structure of HEAs, combined with their unique properties, has sparked significant interest in the materials science community. However, the unpredictable nature of this atomic configuration poses significant challenges in understanding and designing these alloys. The integration of machine learning (ML) has become a vital tool in addressing these challenges, offering new avenues for unraveling the atomic structure and accelerating the development of superior HEAs. This review provides an in-depth analysis of the applications of ML in the field of high-entropy alloys, highlighting recent breakthroughs and potential future directions.

We investigate the possibility of a $X$ particle decaying into three mesons, specifically $D^{\ast}D\pi$, with the focus on its decay into a $D^+D^-\pi^0$ combination. Our analysis of the phase space and dynamic constraints suggests that the phase space for this decay is significantly limited. As a result, the branching ratio for the $X$ decaying into $D^{\ast+}D^-\pi^0$ is estimated to be approximately $10^{-4}$ times the branching ratio for the $X$ decaying into $D^+D^-\pi^0$.

Graph neural networks excel at learning from interconnected data, making them highly effective for tasks such as predicting stock prices. We've developed a novel GNN model that incorporates stochastic elements and uses a differential equation to learn hidden market factors affecting stock prices. The data is represented as a graph, with nodes corresponding to individual stocks and edges indicating co-movements in prices. We've tested the model on real-world stock price data and found it to be a significant improvement over existing price prediction methods.

We establish a connection between the minimal possible size of certain sequences, specifically those related to harmonic analysis and cryptography, and another area of cryptography known as vectorial Boolean functions. This connection is expressed through inequalities that limit the distance between the function values and those of affine functions, with higher bounds applying to functions with higher levels of nonlinearity. These relationships are derived from properties of the function's derivative and its interaction with various types of functions.

This research explores binary matrices with constant margin properties, 
where each row and column sum is identical. We develop an algorithm that 
systematically generates these matrices through a non-traditional sampling 
method, targeting a specified margin value or achieving constant margins across 
a particular set of smaller matrices. Our sampling method can be applied to 
create random binary matrices with constant margins, which can be used to 
simulate such matrices with a desired margin value or achieve constant margins 
across smaller matrices.

which are then used to model the PDF uncertainties. This new object, called the 
reweighted PDF, directly incorporates the information about the uncertainties, 
making it a useful tool for predictive modeling in predictive modeling in

This document is the first part of the ELKI Manual, detailing the entire ELKI data mining framework. It serves as a comprehensive, open-source collection for evaluating and testing data mining algorithms. The entire document can be found at https://elki.algoritmika.org.

We propose and experimentally validate a new method for generating complex frequency comb patterns in microresonators using a single, continuous-wave laser source. By leveraging the unique properties of a microresonator, we can create a frequency comb with adjustable spacing, known as a "comb teeth spacing modulation" (CSM). This is achieved by introducing a modulation signal into the pump laser, which in turn modulates the resonance frequencies of the microresonator. The modulation signal is carefully designed to produce a desired frequency comb pattern. The experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of this technique and show that it can be used to generate a range of comb patterns, including linear and non-linear patterns. The ability to generate complex frequency comb patterns in microresonators has significant implications for the development of new applications in photonic technology, including the creation of new types of sensors and the development of new types of communication systems.

We establish a class of subgroups within acylindrically hyperbolic groups that are stochastic, meaning they are preserved under random transformations, and acylindrical hyperbolicity is an attribute of acylindrically hyperbolic groups. Additionally, we identify a specific class of acylindrically hyperbolic groups that contain such subgroups, and we also show that any acylindrical subgroup of an acylindrically hyperbolic group can fall into this class.

Quantized neural networks are known to outperform their floating-point counterparts, but the underlying reasons for this are still unclear. This study delves into the theoretical aspects of quantization, focusing on models with binary weights and continuous activations, under the Gaussian noise input assumption. By analyzing the network's behavior, we find that binary weights significantly reduce the impact of input noise, thereby enhancing generalization. This insight is further validated through experiments, which demonstrate that binary weights and low-precision residual connections can mitigate input data corruption and improve model performance.
